variants.name: NestJS service method with an interactive Prisma transaction
variants.implementation_notes: The mainstream typed realization: a controller delegates to an @Injectable() service whose method is the script, and Prisma's interactive transaction prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => ...) hands it a transaction-scoped client - every call on tx commits together when the callback resolves and rolls back when it throws. The service method takes DTOs and returns data, so the script stays free of HTTP concerns, and transaction options (maxWait, timeout, isolationLevel) are declarative. TypeORM/MikroORM offer the same shape with a QueryRunner or EntityManager; the explicit driver-level variant remains for raw SQL or cross-ORM access.
pitfalls: External calls inside an interactive transaction extend its lifetime and can hit the default 5 s timeout, which rolls the transaction back.
A transaction client (tx) that escapes the callback is unusable afterwards - never store it in a field or a long-lived closure.
NestJS request-scoped providers change injection scope: a request-scoped service holding a transaction client must not be injected into a singleton.

variants.name: Typed Express handler with explicit BEGIN/COMMIT on a pg client
variants.idiom_name: async function taking a Pool, explicit BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK on one client
variants.implementation_notes: The same low-level realization as in JavaScript, typed: an async function takes the pool and its inputs (or an Express handler calls it), checks out one client, runs BEGIN, the parameterized statements and COMMIT, with ROLLBACK and client.release() in the catch/finally. A Kysely transaction().execute() callback or a withTransaction helper restores the managed shape while keeping the explicit SQL. Choose it when no ORM is wanted and statement order and locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) must be controlled; keeping the script in a service function that takes the client as a parameter keeps it testable and the HTTP handler thin.
pitfalls: After a statement error PostgreSQL aborts the whole transaction: continuing to execute statements yields 'current transaction is aborted' errors - roll back and restart instead.
Typed query results are assertions, not validation: check rows[0] before using it.
A client that is never released exhausts the pool and hangs the service; the finally-release is mandatory.
